content: The co-occurrence of other AIDS-related diseases, such as opportunistic infections, is common in patients with visceral leishmaniasis (VL) and HIV co-infection. Laboratory findings in VL-HIV co-infection reveal that serological tests are generally less sensitive compared to those in HIV-negative individuals. For instance, the rK39 rapid diagnostic test (RDT) demonstrated a sensitivity of 77% in parasitologically confirmed cases in Ethiopia, compared to 87% in HIV-negative cases. The direct agglutination test (DAT) generally has higher sensitivity than rK39 RDTs, but its sensitivity is still lower in HIV co-infected patients (89% versus 95% in HIV-negative patients). Combining rK39 and DAT in a serial diagnostic algorithm can achieve a sensitivity of 98%. However, studies consistently confirm the low diagnostic accuracy of serological tests in this population. In HIV co-infected patients, parasitological tests remain essential due to the suboptimal sensitivity of rK39 RDTs. These tests are particularly critical for diagnosing relapses, atypical clinical presentations, or cases with negative RDT results but a high clinical suspicion of VL. Tissue aspirates yield higher diagnostic accuracy in HIV co-infected patients due to higher tissue parasite densities. Parasitological confirmation is also valuable for assessing treatment response and determining the need for treatment extension or drug changes. Pancytopenia is a common finding in VL, but hematological cytopenias are more frequent and severe in co-infected patients. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends combination therapy as the first-line treatment for VL-HIV co-infection. In East Africa, the WHO suggests a combination of liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB) and miltefosine over L-AmB monotherapy. The recommended doses for combination therapy are L-AmB (up to a cumulative dose of 30 mg/kg, administered as 5 mg/kg on days 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, and 11) and miltefosine (100 mg/day for 28 days). For L-AmB monotherapy, the dose is up to 40 mg/kg, given as 5 mg/kg on days 1–5, 10, 17, and 24. In South-East Asia, the same combination therapy is recommended, but miltefosine is administered for 14 days instead of 28. Patients diagnosed with VL should have their HIV status determined, and routine tuberculosis (TB) screening should be conducted at the time of VL diagnosis, with follow-up as needed. For patients who do not show a satisfactory clinical response, therapy may be extended for an additional course after ruling out other diagnoses. If miltefosine is unavailable or contraindicated, L-AmB monotherapy (up to 40 mg/kg) can be considered. Comprehensive clinical management, including adequate HIV treatment and nutritional support, is essential. Women of childbearing potential should have access to contraception and pregnancy testing due to the teratogenic and embryotoxic potential of miltefosine. The rationale for combination therapy lies in its potential to reduce mortality and relapse rates, which are high in VL-HIV co-infected patients due to the synergistic interaction between the parasite and the virus. Combination therapy may also reduce the risk of resistance to amphotericin B. However, miltefosine is contraindicated in women of childbearing potential unless effective contraception is used. Most cases of VL-HIV co-infection occur in males, and the evidence supporting combination therapy is of very low certainty. Nevertheless, the WHO expert committee and stakeholders agree that combination therapy should be preferred over monotherapy. Clinical trials in Ethiopia and India have demonstrated the efficacy and safety of combination therapy with L-AmB and miltefosine. In Ethiopia, a randomized, open-label study showed that the cure rate with L-AmB monotherapy was 50% at day 29, increasing to 55% at day 58. In contrast, the combination therapy achieved a cure rate of 67% at day 29, increasing to 88% at day 58. The combination therapy showed relatively high efficacy for both primary and relapse cases, with a good safety profile in a population with a high burden of concomitant illnesses and medications. In India, a similar trial compared L-AmB monotherapy with combination therapy. The primary endpoint was being alive and disease-free at day 210, defined as the absence of VL signs and symptoms or a negative parasitological assessment if symptomatic. The combination therapy demonstrated better outcomes, with fewer severe adverse events compared to monotherapy. However, outcomes were worse in patients with concomitant TB, highlighting the need for careful management in this subgroup. Secondary prophylaxis is critical for preventing VL relapse in HIV co-infected patients, as no current antileishmanial drug achieves complete parasite clearance. The aim of secondary prophylaxis is to prolong the disease-free interval and reduce mortality. In East Africa, pentamidine isethionate (4 mg/kg every 3–4 weeks) is recommended, while in South-East Asia, amphotericin B deoxycholate (1 mg/kg every 3–4 weeks) or liposomal amphotericin B (3–5 mg/kg every 3–4 weeks) is used. Prophylaxis can be discontinued if the CD4 cell count is maintained above 350 cells/mm³ or if the HIV viral load is undetectable for at least six months with no evidence of VL relapse. When selecting a drug for secondary prophylaxis, factors to consider include avoiding drugs used in the primary VL episode, the safety and efficacy profiles of the proposed drug, potential collateral benefits in preventing other infections, and the risk of drug resistance. Adequate HIV treatment is essential to maintain an undetectable viral load, as antiretroviral therapy (ART) contributes to positive VL treatment outcomes. However, VL treatment may increase HIV viral load due to the activation of CD4 T cells, necessitating careful monitoring and ART optimization. In summary, combination therapy with L-AmB and miltefosine is recommended for treating VL-HIV co-infection, with secondary prophylaxis playing a crucial role in preventing relapse. Comprehensive clinical management, including HIV treatment and nutritional support, is essential for improving outcomes in this vulnerable population.
